young.html: In 1848 two young Germans, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, wrote a short booklet called The Communist Manifesto. A manifesto is a public statement of what a group believes and wants.

They lived at a time when many people worked long hours in new factories for very low pay, and children worked too. Marx and Engels believed history is a long struggle between rich and poor groups, and they predicted that the workers would one day take over the factories and share everything.

Their ideas became some of the most argued-about in history. Many predictions did not come true, and the countries that later tried to build their ideas set up governments that took away people's freedom and caused great suffering. People still read the booklet to understand those events and the world of factories it describes.

young.html: Then and now. Look up or ask about what work was like for children in factories in the 1840s. Make two lists: "work in 1848" and "work today." What changed? Who changed it? (Many reformers of different views worked on child labor laws.)

full.html: Karl Marx (1818–1883) studied philosophy in Berlin among the "Young Hegelians" and became a radical journalist. Friedrich Engels (1820–1895), son of a textile manufacturer, worked in his family's cotton business in Manchester and wrote The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845). The two met in Paris in 1844 and became lifelong partners in writing. A small group, the Communist League, asked them for a statement of its program; Marx wrote most of the final text, and it was printed in London in February 1848, in German. Revolutions broke out across Europe that same spring, though the pamphlet had little to do with them. Samuel Moore's English translation, edited by Engels, appeared in 1888.

full.text: The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. Freeman and slave, patrician and plebeian, lord and serf, guildmaster and journeyman, in a word, oppressor and oppressed, stood in constant opposition to one another ...
full.author: Marx and Engels
full.work: Manifesto of the Communist Party, Section I
full.ed: authorized English translation, edited and annotated by Frederick Engels
full.note: Engels added a note in 1888 that this means all written history.

full.html: Section I tells the rise of the bourgeoisie, the modern class of owners. Surprisingly, it praises them: they swept away feudal privileges, built world markets and created more productive power in a century than all earlier ages. But, the authors argue, this system also creates the proletariat, workers who own nothing but their labor, and the two classes must clash. They predicted that workers would grow poorer and more united until they overthrew the owners.

Section II answers objections and lists ten measures for a workers' government, including the abolition of private property in land, a heavily graduated income tax, the end of inheritance, state ownership of banks and transport, and free education in public schools along with the end of children's factory labor. Section III criticizes other socialists; Section IV calls for revolution.

full.text:
The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.

Workingmen of all countries unite!

full.name: gb-manifesto
full.cap: The Manifesto's story, then the record. Our summaries.

full.html: Few short texts have had greater effect. The Manifesto became a founding document for socialist and communist movements worldwide. Its attention to economic life and social class influenced how historians and social scientists study the past, including many who reject its conclusions.

items: Failed predictions. In industrial countries, wages and living standards rose greatly after 1848 instead of sinking; middle classes grew rather than vanishing; revolutions came first in largely rural Russia and China, not in industrial Britain.

Economics. Economists of most schools argue that markets, prices and private property are needed to coordinate production; the Austrian economists Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek argued that central planning cannot do it.
Power. Critics warned, from the 19th century on, that abolishing private property would place all economic power in the hands of the state.

The 20th-century record. States that claimed Marx's ideas, beginning with the Soviet Union, set up one-party rule and state-run economies. Their record includes famines, labor camps, mass executions and the suppression of basic freedoms, costing many millions of lives. The Soviet Union broke up in 1991. Some Marxists argue these states betrayed Marx's aims; most historians and critics reply that the outcomes followed from concentrating all power and property in a single party.

full.html: Treating the Manifesto as a description of any country's actual history. It is a call to action with predictions, written in a few weeks for a small group in 1848. Read it as an argument, and weigh it against what happened.

deep.text: The Manifesto in the great conversation

items: Hegel gave Marx the idea that history moves in stages toward a goal; Marx replaced Spirit with economic forces.
Adam Smith and the classical economists described the market that Marx set out to criticize, in Capital, the next rung.
Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality had already blamed private property for many social ills.
Mill and Tocqueville, in this same era, worried about poverty and the working class too, but defended liberty, property and gradual reform.
Is history mainly driven by economics, by ideas, by individuals or by chance?
When a book's predictions fail, what, if anything, is still worth learning from it?
Why might a plan to make everyone equal end in great inequality of power?
What reforms improved the lives of factory workers in the 1800s, and who made them happen?

questions: What was life like for children who worked in factories in the 1840s? What changed it?
Marx and Engels said history is a struggle between groups. Can you think of other ways to tell history?
Why do you think so many of the book's predictions did not come true?
Why is it dangerous for one group to hold all the power in a country?
Is it important to read books whose ideas you think are wrong? Why?

care: A political pamphlet calling for revolution. The lesson presents what Marx and Engels argued, why it mattered, and the main critiques, including the record of states that claimed their ideas, stated factually.
